This error may be because the HTTP URL is larger than 4096 bytes and not specifically because of the Zalgo text in the URL. If you capture the request, how long is the URL?

The error is thrown by Netty (see http://netty.io/5.0/xref/io/netty/handler/codec/http/HttpObjectDecoder.html#733). If you look at [this thread](https://groups.google.com/d/msg/play-framework/LLk8Fkmlj48/2BjPmMNtE_cJ) you can see that there's a command line setting you can use to increase the max size from 4096, e.g. `-Dhttp.netty.maxInitialLineLength=8192`. Does setting that work for you?

I think the problem is exactly as you described it, but I had hoped this sort of thing could be guarded against instead of changing an arbitrarily long number. Granted, I doubt I’m really going to face this in the wild since I don’t think my users will be trying to sabotage their own accounts by submitting Zalgo text, but it’s nice to be rigorous.

Is there a way to sanitise input like this? Should this thing be at the application level, or the framework level? I’m not sure, but I think it’s worth discussing.

Most servers have maximum sizes for HTTP Request-URIs and headers, the important thing is that the server keeps running when those headers come in. The size is configurable in Play, which is useful for applications with unusual needs. However, perhaps Play should be politely returning a `414 Request-URI Too Long` or `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` response to the client when detects a `TooLongFrameException`. At the moment I assume Play returns a `500 Internal Server Error` (but I haven't confirmed this).

There are many ways to sanitize and control user input. This is commonly handled at the application in your Scala/Java/JavaScript code. There are lots of ways to do that. If you're not sure how to sanitise input, can I suggest asking on the mailing list? There's a great community there who are happy to answer questions.

In this situation Netty just drops the connection. I actually ran into this bug a while ago. We had some services that were calling other services with long lists of IDs in the query string. The client was seeing dropped connections, and this error was logged on the server.

Normally in the case of an error you expect to get an actual response explaining what happened. I imagine this error is most likely to happen in production when you have a lot of inter-service HTTP calls, so it would make debugging easier if we returned the proper HTTP error code.

OK I was assuming we sent a `500` response at the moment. Dropping a connection isn't good.

I agree that when we reject a request we should send a response saying what happened, in this case ideally a 414 or 431 response.

We should send the 414 error, with a `Connection: close` header, and then immediately close the connection.

Closing the connection is necessary because who knows what else the client is going to send, it could be a non HTTP client accidentally connecting, or something more malicious, we don't want to continue trying to parse/receive junk.

Closing the connection could cause errors on the client if the client hasn't finished sending the request when it detects that the connection is closed, but there's nothing we can do about that, since we've refused to parse the request, we have no idea of knowing when the client will finish sending it (and we don't want to find out either in case it's junk or an attempt to DoS us).

This exception is handled in `PlayDefaultUpstreamHandler.exceptionCaught`.  The solution will send a netty http response downstream, and it must avoid the pipelining handler (ie, do not send an OrderedDownstreamMessageEvent).

I am trying to see if I can help on this.  So far I can put into downstream a 414 HttpMessage event.  Which hopefully skips the pipelining handler, based from my basic understanding of netty and the code.  On curl and on test using java URL, it seems to pickup the 414 status and connection close header.  However since I need to keep the channel open, so that HttpResponseEncoder can properly encode 414.  When I use Chrome, it just waits on the socket... as it never closes.

Any hints in making the channel close after 414 and headers are sent would be appreciated.  Thanks.

When you write to a channel, you get back a ChannelFuture.  Simply attach the close channel future listener to it, eg:

```
val response = ...
ctx.getChannel.write(response).addListener(ChannelFutureListener.CLOSE)
```

I have tried to do it by sending the downstream an event.

https://gist.github.com/jkyamog/9616210

I think I have the reverse problem.  I kind of need to add a listener to a write, so that I can close after the write.  I took the current approach so that it skips the HttpPipeliningHandler and the HttpResponseEncoder will then write the 414 status.

So if the write of the response is performed in PlayDefaultUpstreamHandler.exceptionCaught so the channel can be closed also at that time.  This would mean writing http responses will be on PlayDefaultUpstreamHandler.

Is my current approach of sending an event downstream and letting the handler downstream do the writing incorrect?

> I think I have the reverse problem. I kind of need to add a listener to a write, so that I can close after the write. I took the current approach so that it skips the HttpPipeliningHandler and the HttpResponseEncoder will then write the 414 status.

I'm not sure whether you should use James's suggested `ctx.getChannel.write` or your `ctx.sendDownstream` or even [`Channels.write`](https://github.com/netty/netty/blob/netty-3.7.0.Final/src/main/java/org/jboss/netty/channel/Channels.java#L670-L672) to send the message. (My guess is `Channels.write` if you want to avoid the fact that of `ctx.getChannel.write` calls `channel.getPipeline().sendDownstream()` and you don't want the write to happen to the end of the pipeline, but I'm just guessing here.)

But all of these methods seem to have a future you can listen to to close the connection. In your code I think it's the future you create with `Channels.future(ctx.getChannel)`. What happens if you attach a listener to that value?

> So if the write of the response is performed in PlayDefaultUpstreamHandler.exceptionCaught so the channel can be closed also at that time. This would mean writing http responses will be on PlayDefaultUpstreamHandler.
> 
> Is my current approach of sending an event downstream and letting the handler downstream do the writing incorrect?

Within the exceptionCaught handler, I think it's fine to send an HttpResponse directly. We can break some rules because we're basically just aborting the connection.

Ok got a dirty working solution.  So I now write to the channel on the event the 414 status code.  Then the channel future completes, I then perform a close.  This happens on PlayDefaultUpstreamHandler.exceptionCaught.  Will do a clean up of the code and test, then submit a PR.  Would need good peer review, make sure I am not doing something that is bad.

We give all PRs pretty good review. What's helpful for us to have confidence is good testing.

I think you could use NettyHandlingSpec as an example of how to test Netty/PlayDefaultUpstreamHandler interactions. This uses a simulated Netty channel.

You may also want another test where you use something less simulated and more realistic.
